Twenty Third Indian Antarctic Expedition
Ministry of Earth Sciences, Technical Publication No. 21, pp 137-148
Contributions of GPS Permanent Station and  
Seismological Observatory to Geophysical Studies at
Maitri
A. Akilan, S.V.R. Ramachandra Rao, GB. Navinchander, GS. Srinivas, 
E.C. Malaimani, N. Ravikumar and K. Abilash
National Geophysical Research Institute,
Uppal Road, Hyderabad-500 007, India
ABSTRACT
On going research activities at Antarctica were successfully carried out during 
XXIII IAE for the long-term scientific objectives of NGRI. The data from GPS 
station continues to contribute to Scientific Committee on Antarctic Research 
(SCAR) and International Earth Rotation Service (IERS). The seismological 
observatory continues to contribute to National Earthquake Information Center 
(NEIC), International Seismological Center (ISC) plays a pivotal role in the Global 
Seism ographic N etw ork in A ntarctica. G lobal positfoning system  (GPS) 
measurements at Maitri, Indian Antarctic station, have been carried out for the 
period 1997 to till date. The International GNSS Service (IGS) stations, in different 
plates, such as Casey, Davis, Kerguelen, Seychelles, Coco, Hartebeesthoek, 
Yaragadee, and Tidbinbilla were chosen for global network solution using Bernese
4.2 software. The GPS data from 1997 to 2005 of all these IGS stations in and around 
Antarctica along with Maitri were used to estimate the time series, baseline lengths 
and their changes and velocity vectors of individual sites. The results have enabled 
to obtain a deeper insight into the driving mechanism and the causative factors for 
Indian plate kinematics. During this expedition i.e., from January 2004 to February 
2005 continuous seismic data was also acquired for processing and analysis. The 
final data analysis of this data has been completed using SEISAN software and 
reported to ISC, United Kingdom as per their time schedule up to December 2004. 
The number of earthquakes recorded as global events and near-events in and 
around Antarctica during the period of expedition is discussed in this report.
INTRODUCTION
The India-Eurasia collision zone has been the focus of intense studies 
by the Space Geodetic Community for Indian Plate Motion. So far space 
geodetic studies by GPS have been made in southern and central India that 
bears on the rigidity of the Indian plate, whose velocity data for two sites fit

138 A. Akilan et al
the rigid plate model within uncertainties, estimated at about 3.7 cm/yr. for 
Hyderabad and 3.9 cm/yr. for Bangalore respectively (Malaimani et al, 
2000). Since Space geodesy can test many otherwise untestable predictions 
and boundary conditions, GPS-Geodesy is extended to envelop the large 
Indian Ocean and Antarctica (Stein et al, 2002). Despite the extensive studies 
to date, major issues remain unresolved. Motions across some of the plate 
boundaries seem well constrained, as implied by good agreement between 
space geodetic and geologic models. In others, apparent discrepancies exist. 
Very few studies have been conducted on the larger oceanic part of the 
Indian plate using space geodesy (Malaimani et al, 2005; Ravikumar et al 
2005). To holistically determine the kinematics of the Indian Ocean Basin 
between Antarctica and India, the data available are very sparse and 
characterization and the delineation of the plate boundaries especially in the 
Indian Ocean are poor. This study addresses several of these issues 
mentioned as follows.
(1) How rigid is the Indian Plate and Indian Ocean Basin? (2) Does 
relatively high level of intraplate seismicity on the oceanic part of the Indian 
Plate indicates internal deformation in excess of other plates? and, (3) Is 
this related to Indo-Eurasian collision and the uplift of Himalayas?
Therefore, GPS geodesy is used to improve the understanding of the 
complex plate motions, diffuse and poorly located plate boundaries, and 
striking intraplate deformation that characterize the Indian Ocean basin.
WORK CARRIED OUT DURING THE EXPEDITION
Operated and acquired the GPS and Seismic data with the GPS 
permanent station and Seismological Observatory comprising of Ashtech, 
Trimble and Benchmark ACT GPS receiver and Reftek Digital broadband 
system and analog portacorder. Due to intermittent failure of Ashtech GPS 
receiver, frequent repairs were necessary and hence as a stand by Trimble 
GPS receiver was installed. In this study, we used data acquired by Ashtech 
GPS receiver up to February 2004 and data acquired by Trimble GPS receiver 
from March 2004 till December 2004 as used in this study. The receiver 
worked continuously and data was acquired. The daily data is of the size of
3.2 Mega bytes (approximately), with 15 sec sample rate for 9 channels. 
Trimble GPS receiver was replaced with the ACT Benchmark 12 channel 
GPS receiver with IGS choke ring GPS antenna. For data downloading 
Pentium III computer was installed and its RS-232 port was used for
